specAnchors.text: understand how abiotic and biotic factors affect the population size and distribution of organisms

primer.text: Every environmental pressure is either living or non-living. This note sorts the two families, then shows how abiotic factors like light, temperature, water, soil and oxygen, and biotic factors like food, predators, pathogens and competition, decide where organisms survive and how many persist.

modules.title: Sorting the Factors
modules.opening: Ecologists split every environmental pressure into two families: abiotic factors are the non-living conditions such as temperature, light intensity and wind speed, while biotic factors are the living pressures such as competition, predation and disease.
keyPoints: An abiotic factor is a non-living part of the environment.
Examples of abiotic factors include temperature, light intensity and wind speed.
A biotic factor is a living pressure within the environment.
Examples of biotic factors include competition, predation and disease.

low.restatement: If it is alive or came from something alive, it is biotic; everything else is abiotic.
low.analogy: A school photo: the weather and the building set the scene, the other pupils set the pressure.
low.examPointer: Learn three examples of each — temperature, light, wind for abiotic; competition, predation, disease for biotic.

medium.restatement: The split is about origin: abiotic factors are physical and chemical conditions, while biotic factors arise from other organisms, whether they are competing with you, eating you or infecting you; both families shape population size and distribution together.
medium.analogy: A football match: the pitch and weather are abiotic, the opposing team is biotic.
medium.examPointer: In classification questions, justify with the word living or non-living, not with vague size or importance.

modules.title: Non-Living Limits
sourceHeadings: How abiotic factors affect population size and distribution
modules.opening: Non-living conditions decide where organisms can live: light drives photosynthesis, temperature controls enzyme rates, water and soil chemistry gate survival, and oxygen levels and pollution push sensitive species out entirely.
keyPoints: Low light slows plant growth, reducing food for herbivores and affecting the whole food chain.
Temperature controls enzyme-controlled reactions, so extremes reduce survival and reproduction.
Water availability and soil quality decide which plants, and therefore which animals, can persist.
Low oxygen in warm stagnant water kills fish, and pollution removes sensitive species such as lichens.

low.restatement: Light feeds plants, temperature tunes enzymes, water and soil select species, oxygen and pollution finish the rest.
low.analogy: A set of dials on a fish tank — each dial set wrong removes its own set of residents.
low.examPointer: Attach a consequence to each factor: light to food chains, temperature to enzymes, pH to soils, oxygen to water.

medium.restatement: Each factor bites through a mechanism: shade cuts photosynthesis so herbivores starve; heat and cold denature enzyme performance, limiting survival and reproduction; soil minerals and pH select the plant community; warm stagnant water holds little oxygen; and sulfur dioxide pollution wipes out lichens that indicate clean air.
medium.analogy: A hiring committee of six, each rejecting candidates for a different missing qualification.
medium.examPointer: Use the paired examples — polar bears and temperature, cacti and water, lichens and pollution — as ready-made evidence.

modules.title: Living Pressures
sourceHeadings: How biotic factors affect the population size and distribution of organisms
modules.opening: Living neighbours press just as hard as any drought: food availability sets population ceilings, new predators and pathogens crash unprepared populations, and competition lets a better-adapted species push another towards local extinction.
keyPoints: Food availability decides survival and reproduction, so scarce food shrinks populations.
A new predator can disrupt the balance and drive prey populations down.
A new pathogen can devastate populations with no immunity or resistance.
In competition, the better-adapted species outcompetes the other, which may decline or become extinct locally.

low.restatement: Food feeds populations, predators and diseases cut them, and competition crowns the better adapted.
low.analogy: A market where buyers (food) set the ceiling, thieves (predators) drain stock, sickness (pathogens) closes stalls, and rival chains (competition) squeeze out the weakest shop.
low.examPointer: Carry the case studies: grey squirrels versus red squirrels, ash dieback, foxes in Australia.

medium.restatement: Each living pressure has a documented outcome: richer food raises populations; the arrival of a predator such as the red fox in Australia collapses native prey; a pathogen like ash dieback sweeps through unprotected hosts; and competition from grey squirrels combines resource theft with disease to push red squirrels towards local extinction.
medium.analogy: A new restaurant opening that steals customers, poaches the staff and brings a food scare to the whole street.
medium.examPointer: For outcompetition answers, name the resource competed for and any disease carried — that is what full marks need.

glossary.definition: A non-living part of the environment, such as temperature or light intensity.
A living pressure within the environment, such as competition, predation or disease.
The struggle between organisms for the same resources, won by the better adapted.
A disease-causing organism that can devastate populations with no resistance.
To win the struggle for resources so thoroughly that another species declines.
